newsitem.title: FRANCE: Charred trucks block Channel Tunnel after inferno.
newsitem.headline: Charred trucks block Channel Tunnel after inferno.

text.p: Six charred trucks welded to the rails of the Channel Tunnel by a fire last week testify to the ferocity of the blaze.

Operator Eurotunnel SA Plc said on Tuesday that full repairs were likely to take between three and five months but that it hoped to resume passenger traffic through an undamaged parallel tunnel in coming days.

A first group of reporters was allowed into the gloomy 51-km (32 mile) tunnel to visit the site of the blaze under the Channel a week ago that injured eight people aboard a train carrying trucks from France to Britain.
The fire, which exceeded 1,000 Celsius (1,832 Fahrenheit), has closed the tunnel to passenger traffic although freight trains resumed last week.

Eighteen km (12 miles) into the tunnel from the French mouth, six trucks remain welded to the rails by the fire, covered by a huge blue tarpaulin. Seals have been placed on the cover by a French magistrate investigating the fire.
Most of the train, carrying 34 people and 29 trucks, has been hauled out of the tunnel.
A jumble of crumbling concrete and broken wiring from the fire stretches over 500 metres (yards), but Eurotunnel said that the structure of the tunnel itself was intact.
"A period of three to five months seem realistic for the work given the current state of our analyses," said Alain Bertrand, Eurotunnel's operations manager.
"I think that, for the Eurostar (trains) and the tourist (car) shuttles, we hope we can have a resumption soon, in several days and long before the end of the work," he said.
Reporters were accompanied by Eurotunnel experts into the tunnel, all equipped with hard hats, masks, goggles, boots and overalls.
Pierre Matheron, a former head of construction called out of retirement to help inspect the tunnel, said the worst fire damage was to a 30-metre section of the concrete sheath.
"The central part has been gouged out like when you eat an avocado pear, but the skin remains with its metal framework," he said.

He said the time needed to repair the tunnel would be determined by how Eurotunnel decided to repair the most damaged section. He said one advantage was that the surrounding seabed at that point was not very porous.

The longest solution would be to change the concrete sheath entirely, something he said was technically feasible. Shorter repairs could involve fitting an extra metallic or concrete shell on the inside of the tunnel.

Eurotunnel ruled out any safety short-cuts to reopen the tunnel. Eurotunnel said it planned to meet a Franco-British intergovernmental safety commission on Wednesday to discuss its request for a partial reopening of the tunnel.
"We are a means of transport like others," Bertrand said. "When there's an Air France crash, the authorities don't ground every plane."
